extracted.intended_audience: Christian laypeople and tradesmen seeking moral instruction (readers of didactic religious literature)
extracted.subtask_description: Didactic/religious counsel for merchants and ordinary people on honest buying, selling, and character (avoiding hypocrisy, extortion, pride). Explains sinful business practices, spiritual consequences, practical preparations, and outward symptoms of vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid religious hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion in itself is not harmed by wickedness, but Hypocrites mix the Name of God and Religion with their evils, using religion’s white to hide the dirt of their actions (become 'whited Walls', 'graves that appear not').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: hypocrites invoke religion to mask cheating (a chapman uses 'Religion' to lull the buyer's senses). Anti-pattern: using pious language to conceal dishonest conduct; effect is delusion of others and self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deal justly in selling even if you were cheated in buying
rubrics_metrics.description: Being cheated in buying does not justify cheating when selling: 'That that which is altogether just, they must doe. Suppose that I be cheated my self with a brass half-Crown, must I therefore cheat another therewith?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom or precedent is no excuse; each act must be just on its own. The page stresses individual responsibility: do not let prior wrongs rationalize wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-gotten gains profit nothing spiritually
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting wealth by dishonest means 'doth them but little good' — worse, it causes loss of the soul: 'What shall it profit a man if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral persuasion and scriptural citation: worldly gain acquired sinfully yields spiritual ruin and temporal misfortune; the writer urges prioritizing soul over riches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonest wealth will not endure
rubrics_metrics.description: God will cast away the substance of the wicked; ill-gotten riches may be removed in the sinner's life or in succeeding generations ('He that is wicked may prepare it, but the just shall put it on').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of Proverbs/Job/Solomon to argue that worldly prosperity gained by injustice decays or is transferred to the righteous; practical warning against short-term gains that bring long-term loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misrepresent product quality or charge best price for worst goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling inferior goods as though they were the best, 'sell goods that cost him not the best price... sell the Refuse Wheat... hoisting up the price; mingle his commodity' is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples of Mr. Badman’s tactics (mixing poor commodity with good, charging top price for refuse). Guidance: give each thing its just value; do not deceive about quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain honest records and do not train servants to lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling a customer for payment again and relying on servants trained to swear to false accounts is a deceitful practice used to extort money ('servants were trained up by him to say after his mind, right or wrong').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: manufactured claims of unpaid debt, collusion with employees to falsify proof. Counsel: keep and honor honest proofs of payment; do not instruct others to perjure themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and prohibition of extortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Extortion is 'a screwing from men more than by the Law of God or men is right' and commonly committed by traders who prey upon neighbors' necessities; extortioners 'have No inheritance in the Kingdom of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: exacting high prices from those who cannot conveniently buy elsewhere; charging beyond reasonable/conscionable amount. Moral/legal judgement: extortion is sinful and will be punished by God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exploit the poor by buying wholesale then reselling in penny measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Hucksters who buy poor people's victuals wholesale and then sell back in small portions ('penny worths, two penny worths') at unreasonable gains are condemned as biting and pinching the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific practice to avoid: cornering poor sellers and creating a monopoly to extract excessive retail profits. The writer urges moderation and compassion toward the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid usury and predatory lending on necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking usury for victuals and pawn-brokers charging exorbitant yearly interest (30–50 pounds by the year on a small principal) is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given of pawn-brokers and high-interest schemes; counsel: do not engage in exploitative credit practices that prey on need.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is unlawful to always sell 'as dear as you can' — use conscience and charity
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling always for as much as one can forces the seller to lay aside conscience and charity and thereby commit various sins (overreaching ignorant buyers, preying on necessity, hardening heart against entreaty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives eight explicit reasons why always selling as dear as possible is sinful (preying on ignorance/necessity/fondness; abandoning charity; enabling lying/cheating as means to profit; violating Golden Rule; misusing God-given skill; ignoring God’s glory; blaspheming Christ; neglecting the Day of Judgment). These reasons serve as moral criteria for pricing behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is unlawful to always buy 'as cheap as you can' — exercise good conscience in buying
rubrics_metrics.description: Buying always for as cheap as possible likewise may force one to prey on ignorance, necessity, or fondness and thus violate good conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry with selling: buyers must also exercise conscience and charity; when lacking skill to judge a bargain, seek someone more knowledgeable rather than exploit or be unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: When dealing with knaves, preserve your own conscience and seek honest merchants
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the author admits one may encounter knaves who sell as dear or buy as cheap as they can, one must not lay aside conscience in response: 'If the buyer therefore lights of a Knave, or if the seller lights of a Knave, then let them look to themselves... but do thou keep thy commodity at a reasonable price.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: if honest dealing fails, seek a more honest chapman or use agents with skill; do not mirror iniquity even when others do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the heart: reflect on the limited value of wealth and God’s scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradesmen should prepare themselves by considering that surplus wealth mainly feeds lust of the eye; dishonestly gotten wealth offends God; a little honestly gotten yields more peace than ill-gotten riches; God watches and records all ways; one does not know the day of death and may leave wealth to unknown heirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five preparatory points are listed to cultivate conscience and deter dishonest gaining: meditate on vanity of wealth, sinfulness of dishonest gain, prefer small honest provision to great dishonest riches, remember God's constant observation, and remember mortality and uncertain heirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule: honest description and valuation in transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: If thou sellest, do not commend falsely; if thou buyest, do not dispraise falsely; give the thing 'its just value and worth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of buyer’s false dispraising to boast of a bargain; counsel to avoid false praise/dispraise and to assign fair value to goods knowingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manipulate market prices through false scarcity, hoarding, or inflating
rubrics_metrics.description: Three specific ways to unlawfully raise prices: (1) crying out 'scarcity' beyond truth, (2) hoarding when poor need supplies, (3) an active hand to uphold prices (helping price rise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: belies present blessing, undervalues God’s goodness, incites public curse on hoarder. Practical counsel: leave providence to God, be moderate, do not participate in price inflation schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show mercy to the poor in selling (undersell in necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When things rise in price, be grieved; be moderate and 'let the poor have a pennyworth' — sell corn and other necessities to those in need at reduced prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit moral imperative to prioritize neighbor’s need over profit: undersell the poor, sell to those in necessity, and expect God to recompense such mercy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your God-given skill to help, not to prey on neighbors
rubrics_metrics.description: God gives some more skill, knowledge, and understanding in a commodity; this gift is not for making a prey of a neighbour but to be eyes to the blind and save them from damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical framing: technical advantage confers responsibility to protect less knowledgeable customers rather than exploit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pride (both pride of spirit and pride of body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride is a deeply rooted sin (early appearing even in childhood); two sorts are noted: pride of spirit (high heart) and pride of body (ornaments, fine apparel). Pride is abominable to the Lord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural citations: 'Pride and arrogancy do I hate...' Pride leads to downfall; the proud may mock reprovers. Guidance: repent and avoid prideful adornment and attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize symptoms of pride (heart and bodily signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symptoms of pride of heart include stretched-out neck, mincing walk, lofty eyes, persecuting the poor, prayerlessness, contentiousness, disdain, oppression of neighbors, irreverence to God’s Word, and praising the proud. Bodily pride is shown by costly ornaments, pleating hair, following fashions, affected gestures and speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These outward signs are diagnostic for identifying pride in persons (useful for moral counsel or for literary depiction). The text links inner heart-pride to visible posture, dress, and behaviour; it treats these as reliable indicators.
